name: CPR / Cardiac Arrest (Not Breathing / Unresponsive)
ordered_steps: Check responsiveness: Shout 'Can you hear me?' and tap shoulders firmly.
Check chest: Look at chest for 5 seconds. If NO breathing or only gasping, START CPR IMMEDIATELY.
Place heel of one hand in the center of the chest (between nipples). Put other hand on top and interlock fingers.
Push HARD and FAST: 2 inches deep at 100 to 120 beats per minute (use rhythmic metronome below).
Allow chest to rise fully between each push. Do NOT lean on chest.
Do NOT stop until emergency services take over or the person moves and breathes normally.
never_do: DO NOT put water or liquids into mouth.
DO NOT leave the person alone to search for supplies if you are the only bystander.
DO NOT delay chest compressions for pulse checks if untrained.
DO NOT give mouth-to-mouth if untrained or without a mask; perform Hands-Only CPR.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY. Put phone on speaker while beginning compressions.
source_label: Based on American Heart Association (AHA) & Red Cross CPR Guidelines

name: Suspected Heart Attack / Acute Chest Pain
ordered_steps: Have the person sit down immediately in a comfortable semi-reclined position (W-position against wall or pillows).
Loosen any tight clothing around neck, chest, and waist.
Keep the person strictly calm and motionless. DO NOT let them walk or exert themselves.
If the person has their OWN prescribed Nitroglycerin or doctor-advised Aspirin (300mg chewable) and has NO stated allergy or bleeding disorder, bystander may assist them to take it.
Keep phone ready on speaker; monitor breathing and consciousness continuously.
If the person becomes unresponsive and stops normal breathing, start Hands-Only CPR immediately.
never_do: DO NOT allow the person to walk, drive themselves to the hospital, or climb stairs.
DO NOT give Aspirin if the person is allergic, has an active stomach ulcer, or is taking blood thinners.
DO NOT give caffeinated drinks, food, or water.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY. Every minute counts for heart muscle survival.
source_label: Based on WHO / AHA Acute Coronary Syndrome First-Aid Protocols

name: Suspected Stroke (FAST Protocol)
ordered_steps: Check F.A.S.T.: Face (ask to smile, one side droops?), Arms (raise both arms, one drifts down?), Speech (repeat a phrase, slurred?), Time (call immediately).
Note the EXACT time the symptoms were first observed (critical for clot-busting medication).
Position the person lying down with head and shoulders slightly elevated on a pillow (about 15-30 degrees).
If unconscious but breathing, turn them onto their side into the Recovery Position to keep airway clear.
Keep them warm and calm. Reassure them continuously even if they cannot speak.
Record any blood thinners or diabetes history for the arriving paramedic.
never_do: DO NOT give Aspirin or any medication (a stroke may be hemorrhagic bleeding, where aspirin can be fatal).
DO NOT give anything to eat or drink (swallowing muscles are often paralyzed, causing asphyxiation).
DO NOT let the person sleep or wait to see if it improves.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY. Announce 'Stroke alert' and state the exact symptom onset time.
source_label: Based on World Stroke Organization & Red Cross FAST Guidelines

name: Severe External Bleeding / Hemorrhage
ordered_steps: Expose the wound: quickly remove or cut clothing to see the exact source of bleeding.
Apply DIRECT FIRM PRESSURE onto the bleeding point with a clean cloth, towel, or sterile dressing using both hands.
Press HARD and do NOT let go. If blood soaks through, add another cloth on top without removing the first.
If bleeding is from an arm or leg and direct pressure fails to stop life-threatening spurting blood, apply a commercial tourniquet 2-3 inches above wound (never over a joint).
Keep the person lying flat and warm (cover with a jacket or blanket) to prevent hypothermic shock.
Maintain continuous pressure until paramedic arrival.
never_do: DO NOT remove soaked dressings (this tears away forming blood clots).
DO NOT remove embedded knives or impaled objects (stabilize them in place with bulky dressings).
DO NOT apply a makeshift tourniquet like a thin wire or string that cuts tissue.
DO NOT release pressure to 'peek' if bleeding has stopped.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY while maintaining firm two-handed pressure.
source_label: Based on Stop The Bleed & International Federation of Red Cross Protocols

name: Severe Choking / Airway Obstruction (Conscious)
ordered_steps: Ask: 'Are you choking?' If the person can cough forcefully or speak, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they CANNOT speak, breathe, or make sound: stand to the side and slightly behind.
Support their chest with one hand and lean them forward. Deliver 5 SHARP BACK BLOWS between shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.
If back blows fail: stand behind them, wrap arms around waist, make a fist above the navel (well below ribs), grasp fist with other hand and pull QUICKLY INWARD AND UPWARD (5 abdominal thrusts).
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until object is dislodged.
If the person loses consciousness, lower them gently to the floor and start CPR compressions immediately.
never_do: DO NOT perform blind finger sweeps in the mouth (you may push the object deeper).
DO NOT give abdominal thrusts to an infant under 1 year (use 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts instead).
DO NOT offer water or liquids to 'wash it down'.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY if back blows fail or person becomes unresponsive.
source_label: Based on Red Cross & European Resuscitation Council Choking Protocols

name: Unresponsive / Unconscious BUT Breathing Normally
ordered_steps: Kneel beside the person. Ensure both legs are straight.
Place the arm nearest to you at a right angle to their body, palm facing up.
Bring their far arm across their chest and hold the back of their hand against the cheek nearest you.
With your other hand, pull their far knee up and roll them gently towards you onto their side into the Recovery Position.
Tilt their head back gently to ensure airway stays open and fluids/vomit drain freely.
Check breathing continuously every 60 seconds until help arrives.
never_do: DO NOT leave the person lying flat on their back (tongue or vomit can suffocate them).
DO NOT slap their face, shake them violently, or splash cold water.
DO NOT place a pillow under their head if it causes chin to bend toward chest.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 immediately for any unexplained unconsciousness.
source_label: Based on NHS & Red Cross Recovery Position Guidance

name: Active Seizure / Convulsions
ordered_steps: Note the time the seizure began (a seizure lasting >5 minutes is a life-threatening medical emergency).
Clear the area immediately: remove hard, sharp, or hot objects away from the person.
Place something soft and flat (like a folded jacket) under their head to prevent skull injury.
Loosen tight neckties or tight clothing around the neck.
As soon as jerking stops, roll them gently onto their side into the recovery position to prevent choking on saliva.
Stay with the person calmly until they regain full consciousness and orientation.
never_do: DO NOT hold the person down or restrain their movements (this causes bone fractures).
DO NOT put ANY object, spoon, fingers, or cloth into their mouth (they will NOT swallow their tongue).
DO NOT give food, water, or medication until they are completely alert.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 if seizure lasts >5 minutes, repeats without waking, occurs in water, or the person is pregnant/injured.
source_label: Based on Epilepsy Foundation & CDC First Aid for Seizures

name: Severe Burns / Scalds
ordered_steps: Ensure scene safety (extinguish fire, disconnect electricity, or isolate chemical).
Cool the burn IMMEDIATELY under cool running tap water for at least 20 minutes (do NOT use freezing ice).
Gently remove rings, watches, belts, and loose clothing near the burned area before swelling starts.
Cover the cooled burn loosely with clean plastic cling wrap or a sterile non-adherent dressing.
Keep the person warm with a blanket around unaffected areas to prevent hypothermia.
Monitor for shock: pale skin, cold sweats, or shallow breathing.
never_do: DO NOT apply ice, ice water, butter, toothpaste, oil, or folk remedies (causes tissue necrosis and infection).
DO NOT peel away clothing that is melted or stuck to the burn.
DO NOT burst or puncture blisters.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 if burn is larger than the palm of a hand, on face/hands/groin, causes white/charred skin, or from chemicals/electricity.
source_label: Based on WHO Guidelines for Burn Care & British Burn Association

name: Suspected Snakebite (Neurotoxic / Hemotoxic)
ordered_steps: Keep the person strictly STILL and calm. Any physical movement accelerates venom absorption through the lymphatic system.
Immobilize the bitten limb using a splint or sling at heart level (do NOT elevate above heart).
Remove rings, bangles, anklets, and tight clothing from the bitten limb immediately before swelling begins.
If possible, gently wipe the bite site with a clean damp cloth; note the snake's appearance (color/pattern) only if safe, from distance.
Transport the person IMMEDIATELY to the nearest district hospital having Anti-Snake Venom (ASV).
Monitor airway and breathing continuously (neurotoxic venoms cause respiratory paralysis).
never_do: DO NOT cut, slash, or cauterize the wound.
DO NOT suck out venom with mouth or vacuum devices (completely ineffective and increases infection).
DO NOT apply tight arterial tourniquets (causes limb necrosis and amputation).
DO NOT apply ice, herbal pastes, or electric shocks.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY. State clearly: 'Suspected venomous snakebite, need hospital with Anti-Snake Venom (ASV)'.
source_label: Based on WHO Guidelines for the Management of Snakebites in South-East Asia

name: Severe Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis
ordered_steps: Identify epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen / Adrenaline) if the patient carries their own prescribed device.
Help the person administer the auto-injector into the outer middle thigh: press firmly until it clicks, hold for 3-5 seconds.
Have the person lie down flat with legs elevated (unless breathing is very hard, then allow upright sitting).
Loosen tight clothing around neck and chest.
If symptoms do not improve after 5-10 minutes and an ambulance hasn't arrived, a second auto-injector dose may be given if available.
Monitor breathing continuously until medical handover.
never_do: DO NOT have the person stand up or walk suddenly (can trigger fatal blood pressure collapse).
DO NOT rely solely on oral antihistamines for airway swelling (epinephrine is the ONLY first-line treatment).
DO NOT delay calling emergency services even if symptoms seem improved after injection.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY. State 'Severe anaphylactic allergic reaction'.
source_label: Based on World Allergy Organization (WAO) & Red Cross Anaphylaxis Protocols

name: Suspected Poisoning / Chemical Ingestion / Drug Overdose
ordered_steps: Identify the substance: keep the bottle, pill strip, container, or plant safe for the doctor to examine.
If the substance is on the skin or eyes, flush immediately with copious clean water for 15 minutes.
Check alertness and breathing: if unconscious or groggy, place in Recovery Position.
If the person is awake, wipe any excess poison from lips or mouth with a damp cloth.
Note the exact time of ingestion and estimated quantity taken.
Have emergency dispatcher connect to the Poison Control Centre.
never_do: DO NOT induce vomiting (corrosive acids/bases will burn the esophagus twice and risk fatal aspiration into lungs).
DO NOT give raw milk, raw eggs, saltwater, or activated charcoal unless explicitly ordered by Poison Control.
DO NOT wait for symptoms to develop before calling.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117 in India).
source_label: Based on WHO / National Poison Centre Protocols

name: Severe Heat Stroke / Hyperthermia
ordered_steps: Move the person immediately to a cool, shaded, or air-conditioned area.
Rapidly cool the person: spray or sponge with cool water and fan vigorously.
Place ice packs or cool wet cloths at armpits, groin, neck, and back (areas with large blood vessels).
Remove unnecessary outer clothing.
If the person is conscious and able to swallow normally, provide small sips of cool water or oral rehydration salts (ORS).
Monitor body temperature and mental status until help arrives.
never_do: DO NOT give cold fluids to an unconscious or disoriented person (choking hazard).
DO NOT administer paracetamol or aspirin (ineffective for environmental heat stroke and strains liver/kidneys).
DO NOT delay aggressive external cooling.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY for hot dry skin, confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness.
source_label: Based on CDC & Wilderness Medical Society Heat Illness Guidelines

name: Fracture / Severe Road Accident Trauma
ordered_steps: Secure scene safety first: turn on vehicle hazards, set warning triangles, watch for oncoming traffic.
DO NOT move the casualty unless there is immediate danger (fire, explosion, sinking vehicle).
Support the head and neck in a neutral line: ask them not to turn head; prevent neck rotation.
Control any major bleeding by pressing sterile cloth around wounds (avoid pressing protruding bone).
If a limb is visibly deformed, support it in the position found with rolled blankets or jackets.
Keep the person calm, still, and covered with a blanket to treat shock.
never_do: DO NOT attempt to straighten or push back a deformed or broken bone.
DO NOT remove a motorcycle helmet unless they are not breathing and airway management is impossible.
DO NOT move the spinal column or twist the back.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY. Request ambulance with spinal board and trauma kit.
source_label: Based on Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Bystander Protocols

name: Submersion / Drowning Resuscitation
ordered_steps: Remove casualty from water safely without putting yourself in danger (reach or throw, don't go unless trained).
Lay casualty flat on back on firm ground and check for responsiveness and breathing.
If NOT breathing normally: give 5 INITIAL RESCUE BREATHS first (airway obstruction from water requires oxygenation).
If still no response or normal breathing, commence CPR: 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths.
If vomits water, roll onto side to clear mouth, then return to back and resume CPR.
Remove wet clothes and wrap in dry blankets/jackets to prevent hypothermia.
never_do: DO NOT attempt the Heimlich maneuver to drain water from lungs (causes vomiting and delays CPR).
DO NOT stop CPR until medical emergency staff take over.
DO NOT neglect hypothermia; keep them insulated.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 108 IMMEDIATELY for any near-drowning or submerged victim.
source_label: Based on International Life Saving Federation (ILS) Drowning Resuscitation Protocol

name: Disaster Evacuation (Flash Flood / Building Fire)
ordered_steps: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: For fire, stay low under smoke (crawl on hands and knees). For flood, move immediately to higher ground.
Feel door handles with the back of your hand before opening; if HOT, do not open, find alternate exit.
DO NOT use elevators; use stairwells only.
Grab emergency essentials only: phone, ID, vital prescription medications, flashlight.
Never drive or walk into moving floodwater (6 inches of rushing water can knock you down; 12 inches can sweep a car).
Once outside, stay clear of falling powerlines and gather at a designated assembly point.
never_do: DO NOT return inside a burning or flooded structure for pets or possessions.
DO NOT touch wet electrical equipment or standing water near wires.
DO NOT attempt to cross flooded bridges or roads.
when_to_call: CALL 112 / 101 (Fire) / Disaster Management helpline immediately once safely evacuated.
source_label: Based on National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) & FEMA Protocols
